title: Hereditary Neuropathy with Liability to Pressure Palsies Masked by Previous Gunshots and Tuberculosis
case_prompt:
A 37-year-old Caucasian man was referred for chronic low back pain without radicular radiation and known disc prolapse at T10–T11. His history was notable for:
• A 1993 gunshot injury to the right lung, requiring resection of ribs 1–3 and right lower lobectomy  
• A second gunshot in 1996 causing a skull fracture behind the right ear and traumatic lesions of the facial, statoacoustic, and trigeminal nerves, resulting in persistent right-sided anacusis, tinnitus, peripheral facial palsy, and hemihypesthesia  
• Pulmonary tuberculosis in 1998 treated with a single drug for three years, followed by chronic bronchitis  
• Occasional panic attacks, holocranial or occipital headache, and no prior episodes of pressure palsies  
• No family history of neuromuscular disorders  

Neurologic examination revealed:
• Anacusis on the right, hypoacusis on the left, right peripheral facial palsy, and right facial hemihypesthesia  
• Neck-muscle soreness  
• Mild distal limb weakness (e.g., finger spreading M4 / M5−, hand flexion M4+, foot extension M5− / M4+, foot flexion M4+)  
• Discrete diffuse wasting and generally reduced tendon reflexes  
• Sensory hypoesthesia of the left ulnar hand border and digits 4–5, and a right stocking-type distribution  
• Positive Romberg with a tendency to fall backward to the left  

Laboratory and imaging studies showed:
• Positive anti–hepatitis C antibodies, HCV‐RNA titer 4.5 × 10^6, ANA 1:1280  
• ECG with incomplete right bundle‐branch block  
• Pulmonary function tests with basal air‐trapping; bronchoscopy negative for active tuberculosis  
• CSF protein 76.7 mg/dL (normal <43)  
• MRI with disc prolapses at C6–C7 and T11–T12  
• Nerve conduction studies demonstrating generally prolonged distal latencies, severely reduced conduction velocities, conduction blocks at sites predisposed to compression, and absence of denervation in the right anterior tibial muscle  
• Transcranial magnetic stimulation with normal central conduction times but prolonged peripheral latencies to the abductor digiti minimi, arguing against a myelopathic cause of weakness
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Atypical CIDP was considered but excluded — “CIDP was excluded, since the clinical presentation and the results of the nerve conduction studies indicated an asymmetric distribution of the neuropathy and the history was negative for previous infection and because of the long duration of the clinical manifestation, the absence of a progressive course, and negative GM1 antibodies.”  
2. Peripheral‐nerve vasculitis was considered but excluded — “Vasculitis of the peripheral nervous system was excluded because polyneuropathy presented without pain and was not progressive and cerebral MRI was not indicative of vasculitis either.”  
3. Isoniazid‐induced neuropathy from prior tuberculosis treatment was considered but excluded — “It was excluded, since it was given 14 years earlier and since it was not certain at all that he had received isoniazid without pyridoxine…isoniazid neuropathy is not usually associated with such low nerve conduction velocities as reported in our patient.”  
4. Plexus lesion was not considered plausible — “A plexus lesion was not considered as a differential diagnosis since the distribution of weakness and sensory disturbances argued against such a diagnosis.”
final_diagnosis: hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
